column1: # The coreutils applets that were excluded from `feat_minix` for platform
# reasons and are in the multicall now: `touch`, `env`, `rm` and `chmod`.
# `touch` is the filetime path: `libc::utimes`/`lutimes` (the port's own
# `utimes`/`lutimes` in `crates/minix-libc`) and `stat`'s whole-second times
# through `std::os::unix::fs::MetadataExt`. `-a` is the step that matters: it
# reads the modification time back to keep it, so it exercises the std change.
# `env` is the exec and signal path: `execvp` with a `PATH` search, `signal`,
# `sigprocmask` and the `sigset_t` operations, all from the port's C library
# (there is no `nix` on minix).
coreutils touch t1.txt
coreutils wc -c t1.txt
coreutils touch -t 202001010000 t2.txt
coreutils wc -c t2.txt
# Reads the mtime back before setting the atime, so it needs the MetadataExt
# times as well as utimes.
coreutils touch -a t1.txt
coreutils wc -c t1.txt
# A symlink's own times: this is `libc::lutimes`, VFS's `AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW`
# and `PATH_RET_SYMLINK`. The link is dangling, so nothing but the link's
# inode can be the target.
coreutils ln -s nowhere thelink
coreutils touch -h -t 202001010000 thelink
coreutils wc -c t1.txt
# `du` spawns a printer thread. A spinning user thread used to be able to starve VM
# (`KNOWN_ISSUES.md` item 63): PM scheduled every forked child on queue 0, above the
# servers on queue 7, so the printer's `thread_yield` loop kept VM from resolving the
# main thread's text-page fault. Fork now keeps the priority `SYS_FORK` inherited, and
# the `du` step after the `env` section is that regression's pin: `env` execs twice in
# one slot, which is the sequence that used to hang.
# `du` reads `stat` through uucore's fsext and the safe-traversal walk.
coreutils cp /etc/group cpg
coreutils head -1 cpg
coreutils du -b cpg
# An environment variable env sets reaches the child it execs.
coreutils env HOME=/tmp coreutils printenv HOME
# `-i` clears the environment, so the exec has no PATH to search and takes the
# port's own `/bin:/sbin` default.
coreutils env -i coreutils echo ENV-CLEAR-OK
coreutils env -u HOME coreutils echo ENV-UNSET-OK
# The two signal actions that need the port's libc: `SIG_IGN` before the exec,
# which an exec preserves, and a blocked mask.
coreutils env --ignore-signal=PIPE coreutils echo ENV-IGNORE-OK
coreutils env --block-signal=PIPE coreutils echo ENV-BLOCK-OK
# The item-63 regression: `env` above exec'd twice in one slot, and the printer thread
# `du` starts must still let VM resolve its first text-page fault.
coreutils du -b /etc/group
# `nohup` ignores SIGHUP, replaces stdin with `/dev/null` and appends to `nohup.out`
# when stdout is the console, so it is the applet that first needed a create with
# `O_APPEND`; since item 71 it goes through the std PAL like every other applet, and
# since item 80 the append itself is VFS's. Note that `nohup` prints its notice as
# `nohup: ...`, so it is deliberately absent from the recipe's "a tool reported an
# error" regex.
coreutils rm -f nohup.out
coreutils nohup coreutils echo NOHUP-OK
coreutils cat nohup.out
# With stdout already a file there is no notice and no redirect: the command's
# output is the caller's redirection.
coreutils nohup coreutils echo NH-PIPE-OK > nhpiped
coreutils cat nhpiped
# `tee -a` is the append path: `OpenOptions::create(true).append(true)` has to reach
# VFS as `O_CREAT|O_APPEND` (KNOWN_ISSUES.md item 71), and VFS has to honour `O_APPEND`
# on the write (item 80). The first run creates the file, so it is the create half that
# would answer ENOENT; the second appends to it, so the count reaches 9 only if the write
# went to the end of the file rather than to the descriptor's position 0. `tail -1` is
# the same fact read back from the file instead of counted.
coreutils seq 1 2 > tee.src
coreutils cat tee.src | coreutils tee -a tee.out > tee.log
coreutils cat tee.out | coreutils wc -l
coreutils seq 7 > tee7.src
coreutils cat tee7.src | coreutils tee -a tee.out > tee2.log
coreutils cat tee.out | coreutils wc -l
coreutils cat tee.out | coreutils tail -1
# `rm` and `chmod`, the two uucore's safe-traversal arm unblocked (item 52).
# Nothing here asserts a message: the shell runs as root, so a mode change has
# no observable *effect*, and the markers are what the recipe's log check reads.
# A `test`-driven marker is the exit status, not a printed line, so it cannot
# pass on an earlier step's output.
coreutils touch r1.txt
coreutils rm r1.txt
coreutils test -e r1.txt && coreutils echo RM-STILL-THERE
coreutils mkdir d1
coreutils touch d1/f1
coreutils rm -r d1
coreutils test -e d1/f1 && coreutils echo RMR-STILL-THERE
coreutils touch c1.txt
coreutils chmod 755 c1.txt
coreutils test -x c1.txt && coreutils echo CHMOD-X-OK
coreutils chmod 644 c1.txt
coreutils test -x c1.txt && coreutils echo CHMOD-X-BAD
coreutils mkdir d2
coreutils touch d2/f2
coreutils chmod -R 700 d2 && coreutils echo CHMOD-R-OK
coreutils chmod 644 no-such-file && coreutils echo CHMOD-ENOENT-BAD
# `/etc/group` reached the image and reads back through VFS's open path: this
# is the file the `grp.h` lookups (`getgrgid`/`getgrnam`, item 52) parse. One
# applet now resolves names (`chown test:wheel` below), and reading the first
# line back is the image-level assertion, one line the harness can match whole.
coreutils head -1 /etc/group
# `chown`/`chgrp`. Unlike chmod, their recursive walk is shared with Linux and
# goes through `wrap_chown` -> libc chown/lchown, so these exercise VFS_CHOWN,
# lchown's AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW, the passwd/group lookups, and (with -R) std's
# read_dir -> WalkDir. The `-v` line is the assertion, and `--from` matches only
# ids the file actually has, so it proves the earlier change took instead of
# restating the request.
coreutils touch o1.txt
coreutils chown -v test:wheel o1.txt
column2: changed ownership of 'o1.txt' from root:root to test:wheel

column1: coreutils chown -v --from=test:wheel 0:0 o1.txt
column2: changed ownership of 'o1.txt' from test:wheel to root:root

column1: coreutils chgrp -v wheel o1.txt
column2: changed group of 'o1.txt' from root to wheel

column1: # A dangling symlink: only the link's own inode can be changed, so this is the
# lchown/AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW assertion (following the link would be ENOENT).
coreutils ln -s nowhere olink
coreutils chown -vh 33:44 olink
column2: changed ownership of 'olink' from root:root to 33:44

column1: # `-R` descends through std's read_dir into a subdirectory and the file under
# it; the `--from` check on the nested file is what fails if the walk stops at
# the first level (the bug item 53 records).
coreutils mkdir og
coreutils mkdir og/sub
coreutils touch og/sub/g
coreutils chown -vR 7:8 og
column2: changed ownership of 'og' from root:root to 7:8

column1: coreutils chown -v --from=7:8 0:0 og/sub/g
column2: changed ownership of 'og/sub/g' from 7:8 to root:root

column1: # `groups`: the current process takes `getgroups`; `groups USER` resolves the
# passwd entry and calls `getgrouplist`, whose list is the primary gid plus
# every `/etc/group` member line (the image puts `test` in `wheel`). This is
# the end-to-end check of the group half item 52 added.
coreutils groups
coreutils groups test
coreutils groups root
# `id`: the default form names every id from `/etc/passwd`/`/etc/group`, and
# `id USER` appends the groups `getgrouplist` finds, so the `wheel` membership
# shows up as `10(wheel)`. `-un` exercises `getlogin` (the port has no utmp, so
# it is the real user's passwd name). The expectations escape `(` and `)`
# because the smoke driver matches an expectation as an ERE.
coreutils id
coreutils id -u
coreutils id -un
coreutils id test
coreutils id -Gn test
# `logname` prints `getlogin`'s name and `whoami` the effective user's passwd
# name. Both are `root` in the shipped shell, and both go through the passwd
# half of `entries`.
coreutils logname
coreutils whoami
# `install`: copies through safe_traversal's openat path, sets the mode with
# fchmod (`test -x` is the assertion) and the owner with fchown, none of which
# needed new port surface after items 52-54. `-v` is the visible line; the
# `--from` check on the `-o`/`-g` result proves the ids changed.
coreutils touch isrc
coreutils install isrc idst
coreutils test -x idst && coreutils echo INSTALL-X-OK
coreutils install -m 644 isrc idst2
coreutils test -x idst2 && coreutils echo INSTALL-M-BAD
coreutils install -d idir/subdir && coreutils test -d idir/subdir && coreutils echo INSTALL-D-OK
coreutils install -v isrc idst3
coreutils install -o test -g wheel isrc idst4
coreutils chown -v --from=test:wheel 0:0 idst4
column2: changed ownership of 'idst4' from test:wheel to root:root

column1: # `mkfifo`: creates a FIFO through VFS_MKNOD (rustix's `mkfifoat` -> the minix
# backend's `mknodat`). `test -p` is the assertion that the new inode really is
# S_IFIFO, for the default mode and an explicit `-m`.
coreutils mkfifo mf1
coreutils test -p mf1 && coreutils echo MKFIFO-P-OK
coreutils mkfifo -m 600 mf2
coreutils test -p mf2 && coreutils echo MKFIFO-M-OK
# `mknod` makes the three special inodes through rustix's `mknodat`, whose minix
# arm is VFS_MKNOD. `nix`, which mknod used, has no minix support, so the node
# creation, the mode bits and the umask come from rustix instead (the pattern
# `mkfifo` set). `u` is the character-device alias GNU accepts, and `-m` is the
# explicit-mode path that clears the umask around the call.
coreutils mknod mn1 p
coreutils test -p mn1 && coreutils echo MKNOD-P-OK
coreutils mknod mn2 c 4 64
coreutils test -c mn2 && coreutils echo MKNOD-C-OK
coreutils mknod -m 600 mn3 b 3 0
coreutils test -b mn3 && coreutils echo MKNOD-B-OK
coreutils mknod mn4 u 1 3
coreutils test -c mn4 && coreutils echo MKNOD-U-OK
# `stat`: the file fields are `MetadataExt`, the owner names are `uucore::entries` over
# the port's libc, and `-f` is `uucore::fsext`, whose minix arm reads `statvfs` through
# `rustix` (MINIX has no `statfs`) and answers one filesystem type. Sizes and inodes
# differ per arch; types, modes and names do not.
coreutils stat -c %F /bin/echo
coreutils stat -c %A:%a:%U:%G /bin/echo
coreutils stat -c %F /bin
coreutils stat -c %F /dev/null
coreutils stat -c %t:%T /dev/null
coreutils stat -c %F mn1
coreutils stat -c %F mn3
coreutils stat -c %F /link
coreutils stat -f -c %T /
# `chroot`: VFS's do_chroot was implemented but unreachable, because rustix's
# minix chroot was a NOSYS stub. The step proves the syscall, the
# `set_current_dir("/")` and the exec after it on every arch.
coreutils chroot / /bin/coreutils echo ROOT-OK
# The jail form is the one that execs a binary written during this boot: `install`
# copies /bin/echo into the jail, and the exec reads the copy back through MFS.
# It trapped on aarch64 only, because that arch's /bin/echo is 77576 bytes (19
# blocks) while x86's is 15952 and riscv's 18600 (4 and 5): the copy's blocks past
# the seventh went behind the single-indirect block, and `KNOWN_ISSUES.md` item
# 60 is what made those read back as block 0.
coreutils mkdir jail
coreutils install /bin/echo jail/echo
coreutils chroot jail /echo JAIL-OK
# The applets added after the core set: `ls`, `dir`, `vdir`, `cp`, `mv`, the
# small unix set (`expr`, `link`, `hostid`, `nice`, `date`, `dd`, `tty`,
# `dircolors`, `csplit`, `du`, `uname`, `arch`) and `kill`. The whole list
# runs in one boot at 512 MiB. x86's fb server keeps a 128 MiB `GEM_ARENA`
# static (`crates/servers/src/fb.rs`) that the boot loader allocates with the
# image, so a 256 MiB guest has only ~25 MiB free and this sequence exhausts
# it (the merged run failed on the first pipeline). 512 MiB leaves room for
# the whole fixture and the fb arena together.
# `ls`, `dir` and `vdir`: the directory listing. `-1` pins one entry per line
# so a step can match it whole, `-d` proves the directory itself is reported
# rather than its contents, and `-a` has to name `.` and `..` as well. The
# long form reads the mode, owner, group and size back out of `stat`, and the
# arrow is `readlink`, which is the symlink target.
# `cp`: the ordinary copy is std's `fs::copy`; `-R` walks a directory through
# uucore's safe-copy.
# `du` ran above, and again after the `env` section (item 63's regression pin).
coreutils mkdir lsd1
coreutils touch lsd1/only
coreutils ln -s nowhere lsd1/dangling
coreutils ls -1 lsd1/dangling
coreutils ls -d lsd1
coreutils ls /bin/coreutils
# `ls` with a pipe for stdout lists one entry per line rather than in columns,
# so counting the lines is the whole-line assertion a multi-line listing cannot
# be.
coreutils ls lsd1 | coreutils wc -l
coreutils ls -a lsd1 | coreutils wc -l
coreutils ls -l lsd1/dangling
# `cp` and `mv`: copying a FIFO is the crate's own `mknodat` arm (`nix` has no
# minix support).
# A path with a trailing separator must name the directory to create.
coreutils mkdir trail/
coreutils test -d trail && coreutils echo MKDIR-TRAIL-OK
coreutils mkdir dsrc
coreutils touch dsrc/f1
coreutils cp -R dsrc cdst
coreutils ls -1 cdst | coreutils head -1
coreutils mkfifo cpf
coreutils cp -R cpf cpf2 && coreutils test -p cpf2 && coreutils echo CP-FIFO-OK
coreutils cp /etc/group mvs
coreutils mv mvs mv2.txt
coreutils test -e mv2.txt && coreutils echo MV-OK
# `expr` is the arithmetic and regular-expression evaluator.
coreutils expr 2 + 3
coreutils expr length abcdef
# `link` is the direct VFS_LINK call.
coreutils link cpg lk1 && coreutils test -e lk1 && coreutils echo LINK-OK
# `hostid` reads /etc/hostid or turns the nodename into an address; only the
# shape of the printed id is stable here.
coreutils hostid
# `uname` and `arch` read PM's uts table through the C library's `uname`
# (`platform-info`): sysname and nodename are fixed, and `-m`/`arch` report the
# machine this image was built for.
coreutils uname -s
coreutils uname -n
coreutils uname -m
coreutils arch
# `hostname` reads and writes `/etc/hostname.file` through the C library's
# `gethostname`/`sethostname`; `uname -n` reads the same file (C's `uname(3)`
# lets it replace the PM nodename), so a write moves both and the image ships the
# file with the name PM reports. `-s` is the part before the first dot.
coreutils hostname
coreutils hostname -s
coreutils hostname gate.test
coreutils hostname
coreutils uname -n
coreutils hostname gate
coreutils uname -n
# Put the image's name back, so a later step that reads it sees what it shipped.
coreutils hostname minix
coreutils uname -n
# `nproc` reports the CPUs the kernel runs, which is one (`CONFIGURED_CPUS` in the
# C library's `sysconf`, the same answer `std`'s `available_parallelism` gives).
# `--all` is the `sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_CONF)` path; the plain form is std's,
# and `OMP_NUM_THREADS` overrides only the plain form. `--ignore` is subtracted and
# then clamped to at least 1, so 1 minus 5 is still 1.
coreutils nproc
coreutils nproc --all
coreutils nproc --ignore=5
coreutils env OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 coreutils nproc
coreutils env OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 coreutils nproc --all
# `test -t` asks rustix's minix `termios::isatty`, which reads the descriptor's
# file type. Both streams are the console here, so both answer yes.
coreutils test -t 0 && coreutils echo TTY0
coreutils test -t 1 && coreutils echo TTY1
# `nice` reads and writes the priority through PM, then execs the command.
coreutils nice coreutils echo NICE-OK
# `date -d @0` reads a fixed instant, so the system clock is not the assertion.
coreutils date -u -d @0 +%Y-%m-%d
# `dd` copies a block, and its statistics go to stderr, which the step discards.
coreutils dd if=/etc/group of=ddg bs=512 count=1 status=none
coreutils head -1 ddg
# `tty` asks the termios backend for the name of stdin.
coreutils tty
# `stty` reads and writes the tty server's `struct termios` through
# `src/uu/stty/src/minixterm.rs`, the `nix`-shaped surface over `rustix::termios`
# (`nix` has no minix support, and the port's termios is NetBSD's: speeds are
# rates, not flag bits, which is why minix takes stty's `bsd` path). `size` reads
# `TIOCGWINSZ`, which a console line answers with the port's console geometry
# rather than with the zeroes the reference leaves (`KNOWN_ISSUES.md` 77,
# `.notes/tty.md`). The
# second `-g` is the write path: `sane` changes `ixany` and two control
# characters, so the save line differs from the first, a read-only `stty` would
# print it twice.
coreutils stty -g
coreutils stty size
coreutils stty cs8 -parity
coreutils stty sane
coreutils stty -g
# The whole `-a` listing goes to a file so the step's evidence is its last line:
# `-a` prints a raw-mode line, and a later command typed while it prints would
# be read as stty's input instead of reaching the shell.
coreutils stty -a > stty.out
coreutils tail -2 stty.out
# `dircolors -b` emits the LS_COLORS assignment; its value is not asserted.
coreutils dircolors -b > dircolors.out && coreutils test -s dircolors.out && coreutils echo DIRCOLORS-OK
# `csplit` splits on a line number, naming the pieces xx00 and xx01.
coreutils seq 1 3 > cs.txt
coreutils csplit cs.txt 2
coreutils head -1 xx00
# `kill -0` only checks that pid 1 exists, through PM's signal call.
coreutils kill -0 1 && coreutils echo KILL-OK
# `timeout` blocks the wait signals, arms `alarm(2)` and lets the child run under
# `sigsuspend`; its platform arm is `src/uu/timeout/src/platform/minix.rs`, because
# uucore's `ChildExt` is built on `nix`. The shell has no `;`, `||` or `$?`, so the
# timed-out runs are a bare command with no expectation: the next step's prompt is the
# evidence that `timeout` returned, and it only returns after signalling and reaping
# the child. `&&` covers the success status.
coreutils timeout 5 coreutils echo TIMEOUT-OK
coreutils timeout 5 coreutils true && coreutils echo TO-STATUS-OK
coreutils timeout 0 coreutils echo TO-ZERO-OK
coreutils timeout 1 coreutils sleep 5
coreutils echo AFTER-TIMEOUT
coreutils timeout -s KILL 1 coreutils sleep 5
coreutils echo AFTER-KILL
# `more`: the pager draws a screenful and then reads keys from standard input.
# Its crossterm dependency selects `mio` for events, which has no minix arm, so
# on minix the terminal surface is `src/uu/more/src/minixterm.rs`
# (KNOWN_ISSUES.md 75).
# A pager waits for a key, and this harness only types when the shell is back at
# its prompt, so the keys are piped in instead. `-n 3` pages three lines (the
# applet adds one to the count for the status bar), the page goes to a file, and
# `wc -l` counts it: the status bar has no newline of its own. The redirect rather
# than a second pipe because a middle stage that defers its write loses it on
# riscv64, reporting EPIPE (KNOWN_ISSUES 79). `printf q` writes the key with no
# newline.
coreutils seq 100 199 > mp
coreutils printf q > mq
coreutils cat mq | coreutils more -n 3 mp > mo
coreutils cat mo | coreutils wc -l
# A second key and a second page: space pages down and q quits, so the page in
# the file holds six lines. Both bytes reach the applet in one read, which is the
# case the key queue exists for: the descriptor has nothing left while the second
# key is still held.
coreutils printf ' q' > mq2
coreutils cat mq2 | coreutils more -n 3 mp > mo3
coreutils cat mo3 | coreutils wc -l
# The same pager with the console for its output: standard output is a terminal,
# so this is the alternate-screen, raw-mode and erase path, and the screen shows
# `ESC[?1049h` in the log. The keys still come from the pipe. The redirect makes
# the exit status visible: a `more` that hung would never reach the shell's
# prompt, and one that exited non-zero would leave `mo2` empty. The trailing
# `echo` is what ends the line the pager's last status bar left the cursor on,
# so the next prompt starts a line for the harness to find.
coreutils cat mq | coreutils more -n 3 mp && coreutils echo MORE-OK > mo2 && coreutils echo
coreutils cat mo2
coreutils echo AFTER-MORE
# The shell's multicall fallback: a bare name that is neither a builtin nor a file in
# /bin or /sbin is re-executed as an applet of /bin/coreutils, with argv[0] naming it.
# `echo` is a builtin, `wc` and `printf` are applets, so the pipelines cover both sides
# in a pipeline child; the direct `wc` step is the foreground fork and exec.
echo aboba | wc -l
printf 'a\nb\n' | wc -l
wc -l /etc/group
# Tab completion and the applet cache: the smoke driver cannot send a tab, so a file holds the
# inner shell's input (`numf<TAB>1000 > /dev/console`). The inner shell completes `numf` to
# `numfmt` from `coreutils --list`, runs the applet, and sends the marker to the console while
# its own prompt and echo go to tablog, so the only prompt the driver sees is the outer shell's.
# Without the cache, `numf` stays `numf1000`, which is not a command, and no `1000` appears.
coreutils printf 'numf\t1000 > /dev/console\n\004' > tabin && coreutils echo TABIN-OK
coreutils cat tabin | sh > tablog
# Menu completion and cycling: two Tabs. The first lists the matches for `prin` and selects
# `printenv`; the second cycles to `printf`, which writes the marker. The list and the inner
# prompt go to tablog2, so the console sees only the marker. Both applets are sorted, and the
# cycle starts at the first, so the direction is part of what this pins.
coreutils printf 'prin\t\t CYCLE-OK > /dev/console && echo > /dev/console\n\004' > tabcyc && coreutils echo CYCFILE-OK
coreutils cat tabcyc | sh > tablog2
# `df`: the image has no mount table, so the minix arm reports the fixed mounts and
# `statvfs` supplies the numbers. The root line is what a plain `df` shows; the
# pseudo-filesystems have zero blocks and stay out of it.
coreutils df /
coreutils df
# The session file: init records the boot and the console session in
# /tmp/utmpx (`minix_std::utmpx::DEFAULT_FILE`) before it execs the shell, and
# the shell retires its entry on exit. `users`, `who` and `pinky` read that file,
# so a record that is missing or whose fields are in the wrong place shows here as
# an empty listing. `uptime` reads /proc/uptime and /proc/loadavg (the kernel's
# load history), and counts the live sessions in the same file.
coreutils users
coreutils who
coreutils pinky
coreutils uptime
# A directory has to keep growing past its first block. MFS numbers a
# directory's slots across the whole directory, and `i_size` is the bound a
# lookup scans, so an entry that lands in a second block without the size
# growing is invisible to the resolve that follows the create: `touch` then
# reports "No such file or directory" for a file that is in the block
# (KNOWN_ISSUES.md item 82). 72 entries is past the 64 a 4 KiB block holds,
# and the final count is what the lookup path sees.
coreutils mkdir many
coreutils touch many/f1 many/f2 many/f3 many/f4 many/f5 many/f6 many/f7 many/f8 many/f9 many/f10 many/f11 many/f12 && coreutils echo MANY-0-OK
coreutils touch many/f13 many/f14 many/f15 many/f16 many/f17 many/f18 many/f19 many/f20 many/f21 many/f22 many/f23 many/f24 && coreutils echo MANY-1-OK
coreutils touch many/f25 many/f26 many/f27 many/f28 many/f29 many/f30 many/f31 many/f32 many/f33 many/f34 many/f35 many/f36 && coreutils echo MANY-2-OK
coreutils touch many/f37 many/f38 many/f39 many/f40 many/f41 many/f42 many/f43 many/f44 many/f45 many/f46 many/f47 many/f48 && coreutils echo MANY-3-OK
coreutils touch many/f49 many/f50 many/f51 many/f52 many/f53 many/f54 many/f55 many/f56 many/f57 many/f58 many/f59 many/f60 && coreutils echo MANY-4-OK
coreutils touch many/f61 many/f62 many/f63 many/f64 many/f65 many/f66 many/f67 many/f68 many/f69 many/f70 many/f71 many/f72 && coreutils echo MANY-5-OK
coreutils ls many | coreutils wc -l
